IANAL, but claiming that Ark: Survival Evolved competes directly with Dungeon Defenders seems flimsy as fuck. I mean sure, they're both online co-op games, but it would seem to me their target audience only overlaps tangentially.

Yeah, I think that's the weakest point in their argument. I think it's a scummy practice, but if they got Stieglitz to sign a noncompete contract, they can likely stick him with breach of contract for working at another game studio, whether or not the two studios are similar in nature.
I don't see how they even have any grounds to sue them. If he broke his contract, that's on him, not his new employer.

Should Trendy find success in their legal activities, Ark could be put into temporary development stasis, and the game could be pulled from Steam until the lawsuit is completed.

I have a problem with this statement. I actually have problems with a number of things in the article, but this one stood out for me. I could be wrong, but considering the statement at the beginning of the article about how Trendy "issued" a lawsuit, the statement I quoted above reads like it was written by someone who didn't do their homework and doesn't know what they're talking about. It really comes across like someone making things up that sound good, when what they really need to be doing is restricting their writing to things that are from a verifiable, reliable source. Like a lawyer.

I understand that in the common view of law in the 21st century, everyone is guilty until proven innocent because it's fucking entertaining or something, but unfortunately the courts are a bit behind the times. They go with "innocent until proven guilty" which means nobody will be issuing orders to halt the sale of Ark until legal proceedings are concluded because it's business as usually until the court renders a decision finding that Studio Wildcard is guilty of some kind of wrong doing and all appeals have been declined or exhausted. In a worst case scenario where Studio Wildcard is found to have been unjustly enriched by their relationship with Steiglitz, justice will be done in the form of a one-time assessment of damages to be paid to Trendy and then life goes on. The court will make a determination as to whether or not Steiglitz can continue to work with Studio Wildcard and then that will be the end of it. (A lot of non-compete orders are pretty draconian in nature, essentially forbidding someone to work in their chosen field for a year or two after leaving the contracting company. It's quite possible a judge will find Steiglitz to be in keeping with the terms of his contract because the genres of "competing" games in question are completely different.)

To say that development of Ark could be put in "development stasis" or that it could be "pulled from Steam" is fabricated bullshit. I agree with the statement from Wildcard's lawyers that the lawsuit itself is disgraceful and I submit to the court that the author of this article should receive a reduced fee for the article and a dozen disapproving glares from friends and family for their decision to pad the article with sensationalist nonsense. The problem with making shit up and committing it to print is that some people fall for it, and some people know better. Then the author looks like an idiot not because they fooled a bunch of people who fell for it, but because the people who know better just dismissed the entire article as bullshit and probably made a mental note of the author's name to save them the time of reading all the bullshit next time.

Those are some good points. What about temporary injunctions, like the one Apple sought for Samsung in their smartphone copying case? I'm looking up some alternate sources for this story, but they all seem to be reporting the same "sales could be suspended" element of the story.

Trendy's lawyers would have to argue for an injunction and Wildcard's lawyers would have an opportunity to respond. The chances of them getting an injunction are extremely slim. First, they have to prove that the non-compete clause was reasonable and that Steiglitz was in violation of in. That would put Steiglitz on the hook for some sort of penalty if they could get that far, but then before they can seek damages from Wildcard they have to prove that Ark: Survival Instinct's performance on the market led to Trendy seeing damages of some sort. If they can prove that, THEN we might see the game pulled from Steam pending an examination into the scope of the damages, though judges are usually quick to point out that if you're suing someone for financial damages, it's pretty stupid to seek an injunction that will prevent them from earning money with which to pay those damages.

It's like a plumber having all of his workers and apprentices sign a non-compete agreement that says that after they leave him, they can't go to work for the competition for 2 years. So one of his workers leaves him in the middle of a plumbing job on a new house and goes to work for the carpenters finishing the frame and roof. The plumber gets all pissed off and points to the non-compete clause in the contract as justification to sue and request an injunction against completion of the house until the matter is resolved. It goes in front of a judge and the judge asks the plumber's lawyers what the deal is. They say his worker wasn't supposed to work for the competition for 2 years after leaving him and because he continued to work on the house under the competition, the project was unjustly enriched.

So the judge looks at the lawyer for the worker and asks for his take on it. The lawyers responds simply, "Plumbers don't compete for jobs against carpenters. Sure, they both participate in the construction of houses, but that's about where the similarities stop. The plumber did not experience any damages as a result of his former worker going to work for the carpenter, nor was the worker in contravention of his contractual agreements because carpenters make things out of wood, while plumbers make things out of pipes."

And the judge, because he's a smart man, says, "Ya, I about figured as much. This is stupid. Case dismissed."

This would be a very different story if Wildcard was actually directly accused of some sort of illegal wrongdoing where it was in the eyes of the court that the accusations were serious enough and preliminary evidence was compelling enough that allowing them to continue business as per usual could lead to greater harm. This case is nothing like that. Wildcard is only named in the suit because Trendy knows that if they want to see any damages (assuming a favorable judgment) that those dollars will come from a business, not an individual. It's a classic case of "technically, we can sue so let's do it and try our luck."
